title: The Constantinian Turn
subtitle: A cross in the sky in 312, and the church woke up favored. What it gained, what it traded, and why the question it raised has never closed.

sections.title: The Battle That Changed the Church's Address
sections.body:
In October of 312 two rivals for the western empire met at the Milvian Bridge outside Rome, and the one named Constantine won. That much is plain history. What happened before the battle is less plain, and the honest telling says so. One Christian writer, Lactantius, reports that Constantine was commanded in a dream to mark his soldiers' shields with a sign of Christ. Eusebius, writing later, says Constantine swore to him that he and his whole army had seen a cross of light in the sky with words attached, conquer by this. The two accounts do not quite match, and historians have argued ever since about what Constantine saw and what he thought it meant. What no one disputes is what he did. He fought under the sign of a crucified man, and he won, and everything changed.

The next year, meeting at Milan, Constantine and his eastern colleague Licinius agreed to full legal freedom for the Christian faith and the return of its confiscated property. Believers who had watched their friends burned and their Scriptures seized a decade earlier now watched an emperor build them basilicas. It is easy for us, knowing what came later, to greet that moment with suspicion. The people who lived it greeted it with tears. Eusebius writes of opened dungeons and worship in the open light like a man who cannot believe his own eyes. Before we audit what the church traded, we owe them this much honesty. To the survivors of Diocletian, it felt like resurrection.

sections.title: What the Church Gained
sections.body:
The gains were not imaginary, and the ledger should be read fairly. The church gained the right to exist. It gained back its buildings and its burial grounds, and then gained grander ones, as imperial money raised churches over the tomb of Peter in Rome and, in time, over the holy sites of Jerusalem. Its clergy were freed from crushing civic obligations so they could give themselves to their work. Its bishops gained standing as judges whose rulings the state would honor, which for the poor often meant a fairer hearing than any they had known. In 321 Sunday became a public day of rest. Charity was endowed on a scale the ancient world had never seen, and the church became the empire's conscience in places where it had never had one.

And the church gained the councils. Only an emperor could summon bishops from across the world, carry them on the public post, and hold them in one hall until they had answered the question in front of them. Nicaea met in 325 because Constantine wanted it, paid for it, and sat in it. The creed that still binds the worldwide church together was written under a roof the empire provided. None of this is nothing. A believer in the year 260, praying through the night before a possible arrest, would have received this future as the plain mercy of God, and we are in no position to lecture that believer otherwise. The problem was never that the gifts were worthless. The problem was the price tag no one read.

sections.title: What It Cost
sections.body:
The costs came in slowly, the way costs do. The first was the emperor himself, standing inside the church's own business. Constantine called Nicaea for the sake of unity, and when the council gave him a creed he enforced it with exile, and when the winds shifted, later emperors exiled the other side instead. Bishops learned the roads to court. Doctrine acquired a politics, and preferment began to shape conviction. The second cost was the crowd. When the faith became first legal, then favored, then in 380 official, the empire's people came into the church in numbers no catechism could absorb. Some came in truth. Some came because the emperor had, because careers ran that way, because the temples were closing. Historians still argue how deep the change went, and the argument is honest, because the evidence points both directions, real conversion and real varnish, often in the same person.

The third cost has a name and a date. In the 380s, at Trier, a Spanish ascetic named Priscillian was accused of heresy and sorcery, and the imperial authorities, urged on by his fellow bishops, put him to death. Within living memory of Diocletian, Christians had begun executing Christians over doctrine. Martin of Tours protested and refused communion with the bishops responsible, because he saw what it meant. The church that had bled under the sword had picked the sword up, and the hand holding it was ours. Not Rome's anymore. Ours.

sections.title: Was Constantine Sincere
sections.body:
It is fair to ask what Constantine himself believed, and fair to admit the answer is disputed. The case for calculation is real. He kept the old pagan title of chief priest. He kept the Unconquered Sun on his coins for years after the bridge. He moved against his rivals with the full imperial ruthlessness, and in 326 he had his own son Crispus executed, and his wife Fausta died soon after in circumstances the sources leave dark. He delayed baptism until his deathbed in 337. A man playing for the loyalty of a growing Christian minority might have done everything he did.

The case for conviction is also real. He legislated like a man who believed, exempting clergy, endowing churches in provinces where Christians were few and favor bought him nothing, lecturing bishops on theology with the enthusiasm of a convert who had read more than he understood. And the deathbed baptism, which looks cynical to us, was common practice in his century, when baptism was held to wash away every prior sin and prudent men saved it for the end. Most historians now decline the clean either-or and describe a man genuinely persuaded that the Christian God had given him victory, whose faith and ambition were tangled all the way down. That reading should not comfort us. It describes most of us. The interesting question was never the state of Constantine's soul. It was what his favor would do to the soul of the church.

sections.title: Julian, Ambrose, and the Limits of Capture
sections.body:
The capture was never total, and the exceptions matter as much as the rule. In 361 the emperor Julian, raised Christian and converted to the old gods, set out to unwind the whole arrangement, reopening temples and barring Christians from teaching the classics. He reigned less than two years and died on a Persian campaign, and his failure measured how deep the change had already gone. An empire cannot be talked back into gods its people have stopped fearing. Julian himself, writing to a pagan priest, blamed the Christians' rise on their kindness to strangers and their care for the dead, and ordered his own priests to copy it. Imitation was the one tribute he had left to pay.

The sharper test came in 390. After a riot in Thessalonica killed one of his officers, the emperor Theodosius ordered a reprisal, and his soldiers massacred thousands of townspeople in the circus. Ambrose, the bishop of Milan, wrote to the most powerful man alive and told him he could not come to the Lord's table until he had done public penance. And Theodosius did it. He set aside the purple and stood among the penitents, an emperor confessing murder before a congregation. It is one of the few moments in the era when the new arrangement ran the right direction, the church judging the state's violence instead of blessing it. It happened because one bishop believed his office came from somewhere the emperor could not reach. The tragedy of Christendom is not that such moments were impossible. It is that they were rare.

sections.title: What 312 Still Asks
sections.body:
When Rome fell to Alaric in 410, the pagans said the abandoned gods were taking their revenge, and Augustine spent thirteen years answering them. The City of God is many things, but at its center is a severing. The fortunes of the empire, Augustine argued, were never the measure of the kingdom of God. Rome was not the church's destiny. No city of man is. He wrote it while the Christian empire was still young, as if he already knew the church would need the distinction long after Rome was dust.

It has. Every generation since has faced its own version of 312, some throne or party or public offering the church protection in exchange for blessing, and the offer never stops sounding like providence. Sometimes it even is. The gains were real, and it is cheap to sneer at legal worship from inside a country that has never burned our Scriptures. But the ledger of the fourth century sits there to be read. The church gained the world's ear and began, slowly, to speak in the world's accent. It gained the power to stop persecution and used it, within a lifetime, to persecute. Nothing in that ledger says favor must corrupt. Everything in it says favor will try. The age of the martyrs asked the church whether it would die for its Lord. The age of Constantine asked a harder question, whether the church could hold power without worshiping it. We are still being asked. The answer is not yet in.

keyFigures.name: Constantine
keyFigures.note: Victor at the Milvian Bridge in 312, the first emperor to favor the church.

keyFigures.name: Eusebius of Caesarea
keyFigures.note: Bishop and historian whose account of Constantine shaped how the era was remembered.

keyFigures.name: Julian
keyFigures.note: Emperor from 361 to 363 who tried to restore the old gods and found the ground already gone.

keyFigures.name: Theodosius the First
keyFigures.note: Emperor who made Nicene Christianity official in 380 and did public penance in 390.

keyFigures.name: Ambrose of Milan
keyFigures.note: The bishop who barred an emperor from communion until he repented of a massacre.

keyFigures.name: Martin of Tours
keyFigures.note: Bishop who protested the execution of Priscillian and broke with the bishops behind it.

keyFigures.name: Augustine of Hippo
keyFigures.note: Wrote the City of God after 410, severing the gospel's fortunes from Rome's.
